description: Hi! I'm a student developer passionate about web development, coding, software, and space exploration. I love building websites and apps that solve real problems, and I'd like to create something that combines technology with my curiosity about space. Join my team if you want to learn, build, and have fun turning ideas into a real app! I'm looking for teammates with skills in UI/UX design, front-end or mobile development, or anyone creative who loves solving problems.
summary: Crescent is a free browser tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates at the lunar south pole in seconds. For any site, including one you click on the map, it computes the real terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and combines it with hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons for 2026 to 2030. A horizon panorama shows the Sun and Earth paths against the ridges. A timeline compares every site for sunlight (power), Earth visibility (direct-to-Earth communication) and both. A ranking with adjustable weights and a mission window finder answer practical questions such as when a 6.5-day surface stay gets at least 95% sunlight and the most Earth contact. A 3D view shows the terrain lit by the real Sun. This matters because at the pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.6 degrees and Earth swings by about 7 degrees, so a few kilometres or a few days change whether a mission has power and a radio link.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Crescent answers two questions for any spot near the lunar south pole and any date from 2026 to 2030: will a lander have sunlight for power, and will it see Earth for direct-to-Earth communication? It covers nine representative sites near NASA's Artemis III candidate regions (Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Rim, Peak near Shackleton, de Gerlache Rim 2, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Nobile Rim 1, Slater Plain). Users can also add a site anywhere by clicking the map.

HOW IT WORKS
1) Terrain horizon: for each site we cast 720 rays across the NASA LRO LOLA polar elevation model (LDEM_75S_120M, 120 m) out to 440 km and compute the elevation angle of every terrain sample in 3D, so the Moon's curvature is included. Custom sites use the same algorithm in the browser on 300 m and 960 m grids (about 40 ms).
2) Sky: hourly sub-solar and sub-Earth points on the Moon for 2026 to 2030 were downloaded from NASA JPL Horizons (DE441, MOON_ME frame, the same frame as LOLA). We correct Earth's direction for the site's 1,737 km offset from the Moon's centre (parallax).
3) Metrics: sunlight is the fraction of the solar disk above the terrain; communication means Earth's centre is above the terrain plus a user-chosen antenna mask. For each site and time window we report percent sunlit, percent Earth in view, percent both, the longest night and the longest communication gap.

FEATURES
- South pole map with hillshaded LOLA terrain, live Sun and Earth direction arrows, zoom and pan.
- Horizon panorama: the terrain silhouette with the Sun and Earth paths for the selected window and their current positions.
- Timeline comparing all sites (sunlit, Earth in view, both), with playback and click-to-jump.
- Ranking table with adjustable weights for power, comms and avoiding long nights.
- Mission window finder: the best dates when a stay of a given length (for example 6.5 days) gets at least 90, 95 or 100% sunlight, ranked by Earth contact.
- 3D terrain view lit by the real Sun direction (three.js).
- Hourly CSV export, and a plain-language How it works page for educators and the public.

RESULTS AND VALIDATION
For 2027 the Shackleton to de Gerlache connecting ridge is sunlit 86% of the time but sees Earth only about 51%. Mons Mouton Plateau and Malapert Massif trade sunlight (about 68%) for Earth in view 79 to 86% of the time. These patterns agree with published LOLA illumination studies, and they show why a site and date must be chosen together.

BENEFITS
Answers that used to need specialist software are available in one browser link with no install or login. Planners can screen sites and dates quickly, teachers can show why polar lighting is extreme, and anyone can explore Artemis-era landing options.

TOOLS
Python (NumPy, Pillow) to preprocess the LOLA data and Horizons tables. The app is plain JavaScript with HTML canvas plus three.js for 3D, hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/AkzoiAlzhn9/crescent-lunar-navigator

LIMITS
Featured sites are representative high points near NASA's candidate regions, not official landing coordinates. Terrain resolution (120 m or 300 m) cannot show boulders or small local slopes.

AI DISCLOSURE
The code and documentation were written with help from an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude). All terrain and sky values are computed from NASA data, not generated by AI.
